title: Store the support portal's passwords so a leaked table resists guessing

blocks.text: The support portal is moving its users off a table of password digests that leaked in a penetration test: the testers matched most rows in an afternoon. Each user now gets one `Stored` row (salt, iteration count, hash). The login service, run by another team, verifies against the same rows with `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256` and a 256-bit output, using the salt and count it finds in the row. Operations raise the iteration count every year or so; nobody wants to force a password reset when they do.
Finish `hash`, `verify` and `derive` in `src/main/java/practice/PasswordHasher.java`. When you're done:

items: `verify` accepts the password a row was made from and refuses any other;
two users who choose the same password get rows that don't show it;
a row written under an older iteration count still verifies after the count is raised;
the login service's own PBKDF2 computation over a row's salt and count gives the row's hash.

blocks.text: The tests use small iteration counts so that they run quickly. About ten lines in total.

cases.says: a row verifies the password it was made from and refuses a one-letter change, a case change and the empty password
the same password hashed for two users gives two different hashes, and both verify
a row made under a lower iteration count verifies with a hasher configured for a higher one
the stored hash equals PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256 of the password over the row's salt and count, 256 bits, and the salt is at least 16 bytes

origin.section: A Password Hash Needs a Salt per User and a Slow Function: PBKDF2, Not SHA-256

concepts: A password hash needs a random salt per user, so equal passwords differ, and an iteration count, stored with the hash, that makes each guess cost; PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256 provides both and plain SHA-256 neither.
